text:
After more than a decade in rented quarters, the Korean Cultural Center in Thailand has opened a permanent five-story headquarters in Bangkok, expanding its stage to meet growing Thai interest in Korean culture.
The center will hold its reopening ceremony Thursday at 5 p.m. (local time), welcoming about 100 officials and representatives from the cultural, artistic, business and media sectors of Korea and Thailand.
Located on Sukhumvit Road, one of Bangkok's busiest commercial districts, the 1,906-square-meter building is the 14th Korean cultural center overseas to move into state-owned premises.
The center, which opened in 2013, previously faced limitations because its leased facilities lacked a proper performance hall and sufficient classrooms.
The new building houses a traditional culture room and lounge on the first floor, a Korean food experience center on the second, dance studios and classrooms on the third, a library on the fourth, and performance and exhibition spaces on the fifth.
Its performance hall features 140 retractable seats and a 271-inch LED stage screen, while four specialized classrooms will accommodate programs covering Korean cuisine, traditional music, dance and visual arts.
The reopening celebration will feature pansori singers and young traditional musicians performing alongside Thai musical theater performer and ranat player Konkan Suthikoses, including a collaboration between Korean folk song "Arirang" and Thai traditional song "Lao Kham Hom."
Visitors will also see "A Landscape carried by Wishes," an immersive media art exhibition presenting two works inspired by the tiger, a symbol of protection and courage in both Korean and Thai cultures.
"Thailand is a country in Southeast Asia where K-culture is widely loved and, at the same time, an important partner in cultural cooperation with a rich cultural heritage and a dynamic creative industry," said Kim Jae-hyun, director general of the Culture and Media Industry Bureau at Korea's Ministry of Culture, Sports and Tourism.
"We hope the newly refurbished Korean Cultural Center in Bangkok will broaden cultural understanding and exchange between the peoples of the two countries and serve as a bridge that strengthens friendly cooperation through culture."
This article was published with the assistance of generative AI and edited by The Korea Times.
